text: Many forecasting methods, especially classical ones like ARIMA, quietly assume the series' statistical behavior doesn't change over time. Two ideas let you check that assumption: stationarity and autocorrelation. This lesson explains both, runs the standard tests, and shows how differencing turns a trending series into a usable one.

A series is stationary if its mean and variance stay constant over time, and correlation between two points depends only on how far apart they are, not when they occur. White noise is the classic example. A series with trend or seasonality is not stationary. A random walk is non-stationary too -- it wanders with no fixed level -- but its first differences are stationary.

The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test's null hypothesis is that the series is non-stationary, so a small p-value is evidence of stationarity. KPSS flips it: its null is stationarity, so a small p-value points to non-stationarity. On white noise, ADF gave p near zero, stationary. On a random walk, ADF gave p of zero point three zero seven, not stationary. On the walk's first differences, p dropped back near zero.

Autocorrelation is the correlation of a series with a shifted copy of itself -- lag 1 compares each value to the previous one, lag 12 compares it to the same month a year earlier. On the random walk, autocorrelations decayed slowly: zero point nine seven, zero point nine five, zero point nine two. On white noise they stayed near zero.

On the trend-plus-season monthly sales series from last lesson, ADF gave a p-value of zero point nine nine nine -- cannot reject non-stationarity -- and KPSS gave zero point zero one -- reject stationarity. Both tests agree: this series is not stationary.

Differencing subtracts each value from the next and removes a steady trend. Seasonal differencing subtracts the value from a year earlier and removes a stable seasonal pattern. After the first difference alone, A.D.F. says stationary, but the lag-12 autocorrelation was still zero point seven -- the season was still there. After both differences, lag-12 dropped to negative zero point three one.

On a series this short, treat the tests as a guide and always look at the A.C.F. plot too. Stationary series have stable mean, spread, and dependence structure; A.D.F. and KPSS test it, and differencing is the main fix. Next, before building fancy models, we set the bar with simple baselines and naive forecasts.
